content: Eryngium foetidum, also referred to by various names such as Bhandhanya, Chardon benit, Culantro, Donnia, Culantro Coyote, Fitweed, Long coriander, Mexican coriander, Wild coriander, Recao, Shado beni (in English-speaking Caribbean regions), Spiritweed, Ngò gai (in Vietnam), Sawtooth, Saw-leaf herb, or Cilantro cimarron, is a tropical herb that can be either perennial or annual. It belongs to the Apiaceae family. This plant is native to Mexico and South America but is now cultivated globally. In the United States, where it is relatively less known, the name culantro often leads to confusion with Coriandrum sativum, the plant whose leaves are commonly called cilantro. Interestingly, culantro is said to have a flavor similar to cilantro. Both plants are members of the Apiaceae family. Eryngium foetidum is widely utilized as a seasoning and marinade ingredient in Caribbean cuisine. It is also extensively used as a culinary herb in Thailand, India, Vietnam, and other parts of Asia. This variety of coriander is particularly valued in the dried herb industry because it retains its color and flavor well after drying. While it is sometimes used as a substitute for cilantro, it has a much stronger taste. Similar to cilantro, some individuals find the leaves of Eryngium foetidum unpalatable due to a genetic predisposition. The species name foetidum, which means fetid in Latin, suggests that Linnaeus may have also observed this characteristic. From a medicinal perspective, the leaves and roots of Eryngium foetidum are used in teas to stimulate appetite, enhance digestion, alleviate colic, relieve stomach pain, expel gas, and even as an aphrodisiac.
